strengths: Well-motivated task definition addressing a genuine gap: multi-round entity-level reasoning for medical segmentation is practically valuable and unexplored in prior work
Large-scale, thoughtfully designed dataset (177K conversations, 168 entity categories, 9 modalities, 5 reasoning types) with semi-automatic pipeline combining manual curation and expert QA
Comprehensive experimental validation including round-by-round analysis (Table 2), diverse baseline comparisons, ablation studies, and ~15% improvement in key metrics
Practical solution to error accumulation: lightweight Judgment & Correction Mechanism (trained MLPs on frozen model) that improves performance without expensive retraining
Clear presentation with effective visualizations of task motivation (Figure 1), dataset design (Figures 2-3), and model architecture (Figures 4-5)
weaknesses: Train-test discrepancy due to teacher forcing (ground-truth masks during training, model outputs during testing) is acknowledged but not fundamentally resolved; JCM is a partial mitigation rather than principled solution

Limited methodological novelty: architecture heavily reuses existing components (LLaVA-Med with LoRA, MedSAM, SegLLM-inspired tokens); JCM is conceptually simple (threshold-based quality scoring + lightweight MLP correction)

Insufficient analysis of JCM mechanism: no visualization of when corrections occur, what features are corrected, or empirical correlation between predicted quality and actual segmentation accuracy; Figure 7 shows inconsistent performance across β values
Missing clinical validation: no evaluation by radiologists/clinicians; no evidence that interactive multi-round approach is preferable in practice; no user study on effectiveness

Dataset quality control details sparse: proportion of data filtered during QA unspecified; inter-rater agreement not reported; extent of human correction for GPT-5 generated relationships unclear; risk of synthetic artifacts

Limited baseline comparisons: most baselines are single-round methods adapted for multi-round, not purpose-built; no comparison with alternative multi-round approaches (e.g., chain-of-thought prompting)

Insufficient error analysis: no investigation of failure modes, which reasoning types are hardest, which errors propagate most severely; Round 8 performance notably worse than Round 2 but not explained

Generalization concerns: only evaluated on SA-Med2D-20M derivatives; no cross-dataset evaluation; unclear transferability to other medical imaging sources; no discussion of inference computational cost for clinical deployment
Missing ethical discussion: no analysis of risks from error propagation in clinical context, potential biases in training data, informed consent for SA-Med2D-20M data reuse

Reproducibility limitations: code/data links anonymized; important details in appendix; no variance analysis or seed sensitivity reported; small val/test sets (1,270-1,273 samples) increase metric variance

strengths: Well-motivated task definition addressing practical multi-round medical segmentation with entity-level reasoning across dialogue rounds
Substantial dataset contribution: 177K multi-round conversations across 118K images, 569K masks, 168 entity categories, and 9 imaging modalities with systematic semi-automated construction pipeline
Strong empirical results showing substantial improvements over baselines (55.8 vs 42.7 cIoU) and consistent gains across multiple metrics, with additional improvements from JCM
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including multiple comparison paradigms, per-round analysis, ablation studies, and qualitative examples
Practical contribution addressing error propagation through Judgment & Correction Mechanism, achieving ~5% relative improvement
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty in model architecture: MediRound is a straightforward application of existing components (LLaVA-Med + MedSAM with LoRA) with simple concatenation-based input integration; core architectural innovations are lacking

Insufficient dataset quality validation: No inter-annotator agreement scores reported for the three medical inspectors; heavy reliance on automated GPT-5 generation (50-80 templates per relationship) without quantifying error rates or quality distribution

Judgment & Correction Mechanism is post-hoc and ad-hoc: Two-stage training with frozen base model and empirical threshold tuning (β=0.6) addresses train-test mismatch symptomatically rather than through principled solutions like scheduled sampling

Potential data leakage not addressed: MR-MedSeg constructed from SA-Med2D-20M, which likely served as pretraining data for both LLaVA-Med and MedSAM; strong performance could reflect distribution matching rather than true multi-round reasoning capability

Insufficient analysis of multi-round reasoning behavior: Limited investigation of error propagation mechanisms, failure modes, or which reasoning types are harder; 'regular vs. hard case' classification not clearly defined

Evaluation limited to proposed dataset without cross-dataset validation: No generalization to independent medical segmentation datasets or unseen multi-round reasoning types; single-dataset results limit claims of robustness

Missing clinical validation and user studies: No evaluation with practicing radiologists/clinicians; practical utility of interactive multi-round segmentation in clinical workflows not demonstrated; qualitative examples show successes but lack failure analysis

Technical clarity issues: Teacher forcing during training vs. model predictions at test time acknowledged but not adequately resolved; history conversation integration not formally specified; edge case handling for small/malformed reference masks not discussed
Incomplete reproducibility: GitHub link incomplete; GPT-5 version and exact prompts for data generation not fully specified; some hyperparameter choices appear empirically tuned without justification

strengths: Well-motivated multi-round reasoning task (MEMR-Seg) with clear practical relevance to interactive medical imaging workflows
Large-scale, well-curated dataset (MR-MedSeg with 177K conversations) covering five realistic reasoning scenarios and 9 imaging modalities
Thoughtful semi-automatic dataset construction pipeline with manual quality assurance and comprehensive categorization
Strong empirical results (58.4 Dice overall) with consistent improvements over baselines across multiple metrics and per-round evaluation
Practical Judgment & Correction Mechanism (JCM) that effectively mitigates error propagation in multi-round chains without significant overhead
Comprehensive experimental design including human-assisted baselines, hybrid MLLM approaches, and architecture ablations
Clear presentation with well-designed figures and logical narrative structure
Competitive performance on vanilla medical referring segmentation (Table 3) demonstrates broader applicability
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty in model architecture—primarily combines existing LLaVA-Med and MedSAM with standard LoRA fine-tuning; main contribution is task/dataset definition rather than algorithmic innovation
Single-source dataset (entirely from SA-Med2D-20M) with no cross-dataset evaluation or demonstrated generalization to other medical imaging sources or institutions
Insufficient analysis of error propagation patterns—no systematic investigation of which error types cascade across rounds or when/why JCM succeeds
Training-testing discrepancy (teacher forcing vs. auto-regressive inference) acknowledged but underexplored; standard techniques like scheduled sampling not investigated
Dataset quality assurance lacks rigor: no inter-annotator agreement scores, rejection rates, or analysis of potential biases from GPT-5 generation
Missing component-level ablations to isolate contributions of cropped images, bounding box coordinates, and conversation history to multi-round reasoning
No clinical validation, user studies, or evaluation of real-world deployment feasibility and safety considerations
Evaluation relies on non-standard metrics (cIoU); lacks statistical significance testing and confidence intervals on test set
GitHub URL incomplete and dataset availability unclear, limiting reproducibility and future research
Small test set (1,273 samples) and no analysis of performance scaling with conversation length or computational efficiency

strengths: Novel and well-motivated task formulation (MEMR-Seg) addressing a real gap in interactive medical segmentation where users formulate queries based on previous results

Large-scale, comprehensively designed dataset (MR-MedSeg) with 177K multi-round dialogues, 118K images, 9 imaging modalities, 168 medical entities, and 5 semantically distinct reasoning scenarios validated by medical experts
Strong experimental results demonstrating ~15% improvement over baselines, with particularly notable gains on harder cases and later rounds (Table 2), establishing clear task feasibility
Pragmatic Judgment & Correction Mechanism that effectively mitigates error propagation without retraining the main model, with increasing benefits as conversation rounds increase

Comprehensive experimental validation including diverse baselines (human-guided, MLLM-combinations, SegLLM), per-round analysis, ablations on threshold β and architectural choices, and competitive single-round performance
Clear presentation with well-motivated examples, detailed dataset taxonomy, thorough implementation specifications, and extensive appendix supporting reproducibility
Thoughtful semi-automatic dataset construction pipeline combining manual annotation with GPT-5 generation, covering realistic multi-round clinical scenarios
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty in the model architecture, which primarily combines existing components (LLaVA-Med + MedSAM) with straightforward reference mask integration; JCM reduces to two simple MLPs

Dataset quality concerns: heavy reliance on GPT-5 for relationship generation and dialogue refinement without extensive validation metrics; only 3 medical experts for screening raises questions about inter-annotator agreement and systematic bias detection

Fundamental train-test discrepancy (teacher forcing with ground-truth masks during training vs. predicted masks at test time) only partially mitigated by JCM; lacks thorough curriculum learning or alternative solutions exploration

Insufficient error analysis: no detailed investigation of error propagation patterns, per-category/per-scenario performance breakdown, or which reasoning types are most challenging; Figure 7 shows relatively flat β sensitivity suggesting JCM may not be critical

Significant practical limitations substantially restrict deployment: single object segmentation per round (acknowledged as F.1), poor long-sequence robustness (F.2), loss of conversational abilities (F.3), and inability to handle 3D data or videos (F.4)

Missing validation rigor: no per-category performance analysis despite acknowledged long-tailed entity distribution; 'hard case' definition not clearly specified; no human evaluation of multi-round reasoning quality or cross-round coherence

Incomplete technical transparency: JCM training procedure in Appendix A is somewhat unclear; β threshold determination method not fully specified; no computational cost analysis for JCM during inference
Reproducibility barriers: GitHub link incomplete in submission; model requires 4 RTX A6000 GPUs for 1.5 days training; dataset quality metrics not quantified for reusability assessment

strengths: Well-motivated task with practical clinical relevance: multi-round reasoning accurately reflects how clinicians iteratively refine segmentation queries based on previous results
Substantial dataset contribution: 177K conversations spanning five reasoning scenarios, 168 entity categories, and 9 imaging modalities represent significant effort and structural diversity
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: extensive baselines, per-round analysis (Table 2), and ablation studies demonstrate systematic investigation; clear improvements over comparisons
Transparent about limitations: detailed discussion in Appendix F (single-object segmentation, sequence length, 3D modalities, overfitting) shows awareness of constraints rather than overselling
Structured dataset construction: three-stage pipeline (entity selection, relationship generation, template integration) is well-documented and thoughtfully designed for diverse clinical scenarios
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: MediRound is straightforward concatenation of LLaVA-Med and MedSAM, closely mirroring existing approaches (LISA, SegLLM) without substantial technical innovation

Critical dataset quality concerns: heavy GPT-5 dependence without specifying human vs. automated content ratio; only three medical experts reviewed 177K dialogues—insufficient for quality assurance; no inter-annotator agreement scores or validation metrics reported

JCM is a heuristic patch rather than principled solution: applies only at inference, masking rather than addressing the root cause (teacher forcing creating train-test mismatch); quality judgment via MLP lacks analysis of learned patterns or generalization properties; hyperparameter β ∈ [0.4, 0.7] shows minimal differentiation, suggesting weak design

Inadequate experimental rigor: no statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or error bars; no clinical validation or user studies; undefined 'hard case' distinction; unfair comparison with SegLLM (trained on different domain)

Insufficient analysis and missing ablations: no per-scenario performance breakdown across five reasoning types; failure case analysis absent; lack of systematic error propagation characterization; long-tailed category distribution (Figure B) but no per-category performance analysis on rare entities

Reproducibility and scope limitations: incomplete GitHub link preventing code access; depends on GPT-5 (unavailable at submission); no specification of λ_bce and λ_dice weights; restricted to single-object 2D segmentation; no out-of-distribution generalization evaluation

Weak multi-round baselines: human-thinking + traditional models insufficient; no comparison with simpler variants (e.g., training JCM end-to-end); limited investigation into which reasoning types most suffer from error accumulation

strengths: Novel and well-motivated MEMR-Seg task addressing genuine clinical needs for multi-round interactive medical image segmentation
Large-scale MR-MedSeg dataset (177K conversations) with thoughtful design including five medical reasoning scenarios and diverse coverage (9 modalities, 168 entity categories)
Practical Judgment & Correction Mechanism that effectively mitigates error propagation in multi-round pipelines, showing consistent improvements especially in later rounds
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple baselines (human-thinking, LLM+segmentation combinations, SegLLM) and clear per-round performance analysis showing 58.4 vs 42.7 cIoU improvement
Thorough documentation with extensive appendices covering implementation details, dataset statistics, ablations, and limitations discussion
weaknesses: Fundamental train-test mismatch not resolved: teacher forcing during training vs. model outputs during testing; JCM addresses symptoms post-hoc rather than addressing root cause during training (e.g., curriculum learning or scheduled sampling)

Limited technical novelty in MediRound: primarily combines existing components (LLaVA-Med + MedSAM) with design choices lacking strong justification; JCM uses circular quality definition (predicting segmentation quality from IoU)

Dataset quality validation gaps: heavy reliance on GPT-5 for dialogue generation without detailed validation; no inter-annotator agreement statistics; risk of systematic biases in generated data unidentified

Single-dataset evaluation only: no external validation, cross-dataset testing, or assessment of generalization to different imaging protocols; MR-MedSeg test set may not reflect real-world query distributions

Lack of clinical validation: no evaluation with actual clinicians, no assessment of clinical significance or practical deployment feasibility; single-object-per-round limitation significantly reduces real-world applicability
Incomplete failure analysis: limited investigation of failure modes, why JCM fails, which reasoning types are problematic; declining performance in later rounds (Table 2) unexplained

Reproducibility concerns: code and dataset deferred to 'final submission version'; GitHub link anonymized; GPT-5 dialogue generation prompts not fully documented; hyperparameter choices lack justification
